name: Slow bulking / slow growth to avoid stretch marks

card.summary: Gaining weight or muscle gradually in the belief that it lowers the chance of stretch marks; rapid growth is a recognised risk factor, but no trial has tested slow bulking.
card.note: Genetics and hormones also influence striae; no trials of gain rate on stretch marks were found.

quick.overview:
Some lifters and growing teenagers aim to gain size slowly to reduce the chance of stretch marks (striae). The idea rests on the understanding that striae are scars caused by the skin stretching quickly.[1]

Wikipedia lists weight gain (fat or muscle), adolescent growth spurts, pregnancy and bodybuilding among risk factors, alongside genetics and hormones. No study was found that tests whether a slower rate of gain changes the incidence.
quick.mechanism: Stretch marks appear to be caused by stretching of the skin, with tearing of the dermis; elevated cortisol, which can reduce collagen and elastin production, is also implicated.[1] Slow gain is proposed to give skin more time to adapt.
quick.risks: Slow bulking itself carries no particular documented harm. Wikipedia reports that a Cochrane review found no evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks in pregnancy, and no clearly useful treatment exists once they form.[1]

lead: Slow bulking, or slow growth, means gaining weight or muscle gradually so the skin has time to adapt, with the aim of keeping the skin of the shoulders, chest, arms, thighs and lower back free of stretch marks (striae). Stretch marks are visible dermal scars, so lifters and growing teenagers who care about clean-looking skin on a developing physique sometimes pace their gains to lower the chance of getting them. A slow pace also tends to keep added body fat modest, which is the stated aim of lean bulking.

Wikipedia describes striae as scars from tearing of the dermis during rapid body growth, with weight gain from fat or muscle, adolescent growth spurts, pregnancy and bodybuilding among the listed risk factors, alongside genetics and raised cortisol.[1] The slow-growth idea follows from that mechanism. No published trial has compared different rates of weight or muscle gain with stretch mark incidence.

On looksmax.org, gradual bulking is usually discussed as lean bulking: a modest calorie surplus aimed at adding muscle without looking soft or bloated, with stretch marks mentioned less often than body composition.[2][3]

paras: Stretch marks are scars from tearing of the dermis during rapid growth. Higher levels of cortisone reduce skin pliability and can stop fibroblasts from making the collagen and elastin that keep skin taut.[1] Corticosteroid use and conditions such as Cushing's syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome may raise the likelihood.[1]

Risk factors listed include weight gain from fat or muscle, adolescent growth spurts, pregnancy, bodybuilding and hormone replacement therapy. In pregnancy, a 2006 study of 324 women linked striae with young maternal age, high BMI, gestational weight gain over 15 kg and higher birth weight, and genetics including family history appear predictive.[1]

Proponents of gradual gain reason that a smaller rate of change gives the skin time to adapt. This reasoning is consistent with the stretching mechanism but has not been tested directly in trials of gain rate. Nutrition (zinc, protein and vitamins A, C and D) is suggested on Wikipedia as potentially helpful, though it is described as a suggestion rather than established prevention.[1]

In bodybuilding, bulking is the off-season phase in which lifters eat in a calorie surplus to build muscle; a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more body fat. Clean or lean bulking aims to add muscle with little fat gain, takes longer and relies on meeting daily calorie targets, whereas dirty bulking uses large surpluses and adds muscle quickly together with more fat.[5] Wikipedia's bodybuilding article gives typical muscle gains for a novice lifting about seven hours a week as roughly 4 to 7 kg per year, slowing to about 2 to 7 kg per year after two years and 1 to 5 kg per year after five.[5] Because skin has to accommodate whatever tissue is added, the pace of gain in the first years is the stage at which the slow-growth idea is most often applied.

Wikipedia lists weight gain from fat or muscle, adolescent growth spurts and bodybuilding among the circumstances in which stretch marks are common.[1] The NHS lists puberty, fast weight loss or gain, being overweight, steroid creams or tablets and a family history as higher-risk situations, and says stretch marks cannot always be prevented, while keeping a healthy weight lowers the chance of getting them.[6]

Forum threads about lean bulking ask how large a calorie surplus to use to gain muscle without fat, for example a daily surplus of about 500 kcal suggested by one poster who wanted to go from 155 to 165 lb without looking chubby.[2] Teenage posters ask about supplements and about whether bulking will make them fat during growth.[3][4] Stretch marks are a secondary concern in these discussions, which centre on keeping a lean look.

A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found no evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks in pregnancy, and a 2014 review found no clearly useful treatment for established marks. Topical tretinoin has been effective in several studies on early marks, but is a teratogen and is not used in pregnancy.[1]

The NHS describes stretch marks as common and harmless, usually starting pink, red, brown, black, silver or purple and tending to fade without always disappearing. It notes that many creams and lotions lack good evidence, that retinoids or hyaluronic acid may help newer marks, and that light, laser and microdermabrasion treatments can improve their look without removing them.[6]

Wikipedia notes that stretch marks are most likely on areas where more fat is stored, such as the abdomen, upper arms, back, thighs and hips, and that some reports describe people of Asian descent as more prone.[1] Striae were first recognised by Roederer in 1773 and histologically described in 1889.[1]
No studies found examining slow versus rapid bulking and stretch mark incidence. Related research on pregnancy and adolescent growth is summarised above.[1]

timeline.event: Striae described histologically by Troisier and Ménétrier.[1]

lore.intro: Lean bulking is a common topic on looksmax.org, where users weigh adding muscle against gaining visible fat; stretch marks appear mainly as a side consideration for fast gainers.[2][3]

claims.claim: A slow, small surplus builds muscle without getting fat or soft-looking
claims.believers: Posters planning a lean bulk propose small daily surpluses to avoid looking bloated.[2] Others say staying in a permanent lean bulk means always carrying some fat in exchange for muscle.[3]
claims.experts: No published trial has compared lean and faster bulking for appearance outcomes in these forum scenarios; the entry's own evidence concerns skin and stretch marks.

claims.claim: Gaining slowly lowers the chance of stretch marks
claims.believers: The reasoning is that a smaller rate of change gives skin time to adapt.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports striae result from rapid growth and tearing of the dermis, with genetics and hormones also influencing risk; no trial has tested gain rate.[1]

claims.claim: Staying in a permanent lean bulk means always carrying some fat
claims.believers: One forum reply holds that a natural lifter in a perma lean bulk will always have some bloating and fat, trading that for a fuller look.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's bodybuilding article describes some fat gain as expected during a bulk, with larger surpluses adding more.[5]

chain: Weight and muscle are gained gradually
Skin stretches more slowly and has time to adapt
Lower chance of visible striae on shoulders, chest and thighs
angle.text: Lifters and teenagers pace their gains so that new muscle shows without stretch-mark scarring. The idea matches the stretching mechanism for striae and also keeps fat gain small, which many people want for a lean look.
